127.title: Fasting explained, never assigned
127.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep vratas, vows that often include fasting, on particular weekdays, festivals or lunar days: some eat only fruit and milk, some one meal, some abstain from grains, and a few go without water; children, elders, the sick and pregnant women are commonly excused.

segments.voice: Yesterday, surya namaskar, a bow to the sun in movement and breath. Your line was bow to the sun.

A coworker turns down the office pizza on a Monday. Not a diet, she says: it's my Monday fast. Another friend eats only fruit for nine days every autumn. Someone's aunt goes all day without even water, and at moonrise the whole family gathers on the roof to watch her break it. From the outside it can look strange, even a little extreme. The people keeping these fasts often describe them very differently. So what's going on? First, a promise: nobody here is going to tell you to fast. Today is about what a fast is for.
screen: `A MONDAY FAST, NINE DAYS OF FRUIT.` → `WHY DO PEOPLE CHOOSE THIS?` → `EXPLAINED, NEVER ASSIGNED.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is vrata, a vow. That's the first surprise: in Hindu practice, a fast is often one way of keeping a vow, not the other way round. A vrata is a promise made for a purpose, for a set time, often to a particular form of the divine. Mondays, for some, are for Shiva. Some fasts come with festivals, like the nine nights of Navaratri. On Karva Chauth, married women in parts of North India traditionally fast from sunrise until the moon comes up. There are many ways to keep one. The strictest is without even water. Gentler forms mean only fruit and milk, one simple meal, giving up grains, or a single food for the day. Another word for fasting is upavasa, which people explain as staying near: near the divine, near the intention. So what does a vow-fast do? It turns hunger into a reminder. Every time your stomach speaks, you remember why you chose this. The hunger isn't punishment; it's a bell that keeps ringing all day. It trains the will: you find out you can say no to yourself, gently, and survive. And it often ends in sharing, broken with prasad, with family, around a table. The tradition itself is careful here. Children, elders, the sick and pregnant women are commonly excused, and others keep a light version. A fast that harms the body breaks the line from two days ago: this is where you live. The key word is the one in your carry: chosen.
screen: `VRATA — A VOW, NOT JUST A FAST.` · `FRUIT, ONE MEAL, OR NO WATER.` · `UPAVASA: STAYING NEAR.` · `HUNGER BECOMES A BELL.`

segments.voice: No fasting required, and if food is complicated for you, leave food out of this completely. Choose one small thing to skip for the rest of today, a snack, sugar in your tea, or something that isn't food at all, like an hour of scrolling or one complaint, small enough to keep. Give it a purpose, who or what it's for, and hold that for a moment; when you miss it later, let it bring you back here.
Vrata. A vow: a promise kept for a purpose and a set time, often by fasting, where the hunger becomes a reminder. Today's word.
Your line: chosen hunger. The hunger is a bell, not a punishment. That's day one hundred twenty-seven.

128.title: Sattvic
128.hook: food that calms; not a diet, a lens
128.howItsDone: Many Hindus aim for sattvic meals, fresh, simple and often vegetarian, and some also avoid onion, garlic and alcohol, especially on festival days, fast days or in temple kitchens; practices differ widely by family and community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vrata, the vow kept for a purpose and a set time. Your line was chosen hunger.

Two meals. The first: a huge, greasy late-night order, eaten fast on the couch while a show plays and a phone buzzes. Afterward: heavy, a little foggy, and somehow still restless. The second: a simple bowl of something warm, rice, lentils, a few vegetables, eaten slowly at a table by a window. Afterward: steady. Clear. Ready to sit quietly for a while. No nutrition label needed to tell them apart. An old Hindu idea gives that difference a name. Today: sattvic.
screen: `A HEAVY, RUSHED MEAL.` → `A SIMPLE BOWL BY A WINDOW.` → `TWO MEALS, TWO AFTERWARDS.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavad Gita describes nature as woven from three qualities, the gunas. Sattva is clarity, balance, light. Rajas is energy, drive, restlessness. Tamas is heaviness, dullness, inertia. The Gita says they take turns prevailing, one rising over the other two. Sattvic means full of sattva. In its seventeenth chapter, the Gita applies this to food. Food the sattvic love increases life, strength, health and joy: fresh, wholesome, nourishing, pleasant. Food the rajasic crave is too bitter, too sour, too salty, too hot and burning, and brings pain and unease. Food dear to the tamasic is stale, tasteless, spoiled, or left over too long. In practice, sattvic food is often taken to mean fresh, simple, vegetarian meals, and some also avoid onion and garlic, often counted as stirring or dulling. Families and communities differ on the details, and not every Hindu is vegetarian. Here's why it's a lens, not a diet. The question isn't only what's on the plate. It's what the meal does to your mind. Food cooked in a rage, gulped in a hurry, eaten while arguing, is hard to call calm, however healthy it is. So sattvic is also a way of eating: fresh, at a steady pace, with some gratitude. You don't have to change your menu to try it. Just ask of any meal: will this leave me clearer, or cloudier?
screen: `THREE GUNAS: CLARITY, DRIVE, DULLNESS.` · `THE GITA'S THREE KINDS OF FOOD.` · `FRESH, SIMPLE, OFTEN VEGETARIAN.` · `NOT A DIET: A LENS.`

segments.voice: If there's a small bite near you, a piece of fruit, a nut, a sip of tea, take it now; if not, picture your next meal, and before you eat, look at it and ask where it came from. Eat one bite much more slowly than usual, noticing the taste, the texture, the warmth, and put it down between bites. When you've finished, sit and notice how your body and mind feel: clearer, heavier, or the same.
Sattvic. Full of sattva, clarity: food, and a way of eating, that leaves the mind calm and clear. Today's word.
Your line: eat quiet. How you eat counts as much as what is on the plate. Until tomorrow.

129.title: The first haircut
129.hook: a wailing toddler, a fast barber and a grandmother catching every curl: why a first haircut is a holy day
129.howItsDone: Many Hindu families keep some of the samskaras: a naming ceremony, the first feeding of rice (annaprashana), the first haircut (mundan or chudakarana), often at a temple, and a first-letters ceremony honoring Saraswati.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sattvic: food that leaves you clearer. Your line was eat quiet. Today, a baby's first bite of rice, and a first haircut.

A temple courtyard, early morning. A toddler sits on an uncle's lap, wailing. A barber with a razor works fast. Grandma holds a cloth to catch every curl, and someone is filming on two phones at once. Ten minutes later the child is bald, dabbed with cool sandalwood paste, eating a sweet, and has completely forgotten the whole thing. The family hasn't. They'll tell the story for years. Why shave a baby's head? And why does it count as a holy day?
screen: `A TODDLER, A RAZOR, A GRANDMOTHER.` → `BALD, AND EATING A SWEET.` → `WHY IS THIS HOLY?`

segments.voice: It's a samskara. The word means a finishing, a polishing, the way raw metal is worked until it shines. In Hindu life, the samskaras are the rites that mark the steps of a person's life, from before birth to after death. Later lists often count sixteen, though the lists differ, and most families keep only some. Here are a few you may have been through without knowing their names. Namakarana, the naming, often on the eleventh or twelfth day after birth. Annaprashana, the first bite of solid food, usually rice, at around six months; the old household manuals set it in the sixth month. Chudakarana, the first haircut, which many families call mundan, in the first or third year by family custom. The hair the baby was born with is shaved away, a fresh start, and many families offer it at a temple or a holy river. Vidyarambha, the start of learning: a child traces the first letters, often in a plate of rice, often on a day for Saraswati, the goddess of learning. It's why so many kids were taught that if you step on a book, you touch it and then your forehead: books belong to Saraswati. And the biggest samskara of all, the wedding, gets its own day soon. Notice what all of these do. They take a body, small and ordinary and growing, and stop the whole family to say: this step matters. Nobody's first haircut has to be holy. A samskara makes it so, on purpose.
screen: `SAMSKARA — A POLISHING.` · `A NAME, A FIRST BITE OF RICE.` · `THE FIRST HAIRCUT, GIVEN AWAY.` · `FIRST LETTERS, AND THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Remember a first that someone marked for you: a first day of school, a first bike ride, a birthday, a photo someone kept, and picture who was there and who made the fuss. You may only remember the story told about it, and that's fine; breathe in the fact that someone thought your small step was worth stopping for. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.
Samskara. A polishing: the family rites that mark the steps of a life, from a name to a first bite of rice to a first haircut. Today's word.
Your line: this step matters. A family stops, and an ordinary day becomes a holy one. Day one hundred twenty-nine, marked.

130.title: Ekadashi
130.howItsDone: Many Hindus, especially devotees of Vishnu and Krishna, observe Ekadashi, the eleventh lunar day of each fortnight, by avoiding grains and beans or fasting, spending extra time in prayer or singing, and breaking the fast the next morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, samskara: a first bite of rice, a first haircut, a family stopping to mark the step. Your line was this step matters.

On the kitchen wall hangs a paper calendar, often a free one from the local Indian grocery store, with a picture of a god at the top. Every day has tiny print: the phase of the moon, festival names. And about twice a month, one day is marked, sometimes circled in pen. Grandma circled it. No rice in the house that day. Maybe no food until evening. Nobody made an announcement; everybody just knew. Yesterday was about food shared. Today, food set down on a schedule. Today: Ekadashi.
screen: `THE PAPER CALENDAR IN THE KITCHEN.` → `ONE DAY CIRCLED, TWICE A MONTH.` → `TODAY: EKADASHI.`

segments.voice: Ekadashi means the eleventh: eka is one, dasha is ten. The Hindu calendar follows the moon, and each lunar month has two halves, called fortnights: the bright half, as the moon grows toward full, and the dark half, as it shrinks toward new. Each half has fifteen lunar days, and the eleventh day of each half is Ekadashi. So it comes about twice a month, and because it follows the moon, it lands on a different date on your wall calendar every time. Ekadashi is especially dear to devotees of Vishnu and Krishna. One of the Puranas tells a story about it: Ekadashi was a power, pictured as a goddess, who came out of Vishnu to defeat a demon while he rested, and was given this day in return. How is it kept? It's the vrata from three days ago, on a rhythm. Those who keep it often avoid grains and beans for the day, eating fruit, milk, nuts, or foods made from certain flours instead. Some fast fully. A few keep one Ekadashi a year without even water. The fast is usually broken the next morning, often at a set time, and the day is often given to extra prayer, singing, or reading. Here's the gift of it. A one-off vow depends on remembering. A rhythm carries you. Twice a month, with the moon, the day comes around whether you're in the mood or not, and it becomes part of how a household breathes.
screen: `EKA + DASHA: THE ELEVENTH.` · `TWO HALVES OF EVERY LUNAR MONTH.` · `DEAR TO VISHNU; NO GRAINS.` · `A VOW REMEMBERED; A RHYTHM CARRIES.`

segments.voice: Think back to the last time you noticed the moon: a thin sliver, half, nearly full? If you don't remember, that's fine. Then think of the rhythms that carry you without effort, Sunday calls, Friday dinners, a monthly visit, and notice how they keep coming around without a fresh decision each time; no fasting needed, and if you'd like one more rhythm, the moon is always offering it.
Ekadashi. The eleventh day of each half of the lunar month, twice a month, kept as a fast day, especially by devotees of Vishnu. Today's word.
Your line: a rhythm. Twice a month, the moon brings it back. That's one hundred thirty.

131.title: The dot on the forehead
131.hook: a red thumbprint from the temple, three lines of ash, a sticker bindi at a wedding: what the forehead mark means
131.carry: a mark of what you honor
131.howItsDone: Many Hindus wear a tilak of kumkum, sandalwood paste or sacred ash, daily or after temple worship, its shape often showing their lineage; many women and girls wear a bindi, and in many North Indian families married women wear sindoor in the hair parting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ekadashi, the eleventh day of the moon. Your line was a rhythm. Today the week closes on something people can see from across the room.

Monday morning. A coworker squints and says, kindly, you've got something on your forehead. You stopped at the temple on the way in, and the priest's red thumbprint is still there. You'll have seen other versions. A grandmother's neat red dot. Three white lines of ash on a man at the temple. A cousin's glittering sticker bindi at a wedding. A week about the body as the place you live closes on the one mark people wear on the outside. Today: the tilak.
screen: `SOMETHING ON YOUR FOREHEAD.` → `A RED DOT, THREE LINES OF ASH.` → `THE MARK ON THE OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Tilak is the everyday word for a mark on the forehead. It's made from a few things: kumkum, a red powder made from turmeric; sandalwood paste, cool and fragrant; or sacred ash, called vibhuti. The shape can tell you something about a person's lineage. Three horizontal lines of ash are worn by many devotees of Shiva. A tall U or V shape, often with a line down the middle, by many devotees of Vishnu and Krishna. A red dot by many devotees of the Goddess, and by many others too. And plenty of Hindus wear no mark at all, or only on temple days. Bindi means a dot, from bindu, a point. Many women and girls wear one, red or any color, painted or stuck on. A bindi doesn't by itself mean someone is married. In many North Indian families, it's the red line of sindoor in the parting of the hair that marks a married woman, and you'll see it again at the wedding. Why the forehead, between the eyebrows? In yoga texts, that's the place of a center called ajna, linked with attention and insight. Many people say the mark is a small reminder to look out from there. And often it's given, not put on: by a priest after puja, by an elder before a journey, by a sister on Raksha Bandhan. So when the coworker asks, there's a short, true answer. It's a tilak. It's a blessing, and it shows what I honor.

segments.voice: Close your eyes, breathe slowly, and without straining let your attention settle between your eyebrows, where a tilak would go, as if a cool fingertip of sandalwood were resting there; when the mind wanders, come back to that spot. If you pray, you can hold there the form of God you honor. If you don't, simply look out from there for a while.

132.title: The temple, explained
132.howItsDone: Visitors to a Hindu temple remove their shoes at the entrance, often wash their hands and ring the bell, then approach the inner shrine to see and bow to the murti, visiting smaller shrines and receiving prasad; most people come and go at any time, with crowds at arti times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tilak: ash, sandalwood or red powder on the forehead. Your line was a mark of what you honor.
screen: `TILAK — A MARK OF WHAT YOU HONOR.`

segments.voice: You're standing outside a Hindu temple for the first time. Maybe it's a grand carved one, maybe a converted warehouse off the highway with a painted sign. People go in and out, easy and relaxed. And you're frozen at the steps. Do I need to be Hindu? What do I wear? Where do I go first? What if I do something wrong in front of everyone? For weeks you've practiced at home: the shrine, the flame, the food. This week you step out of the house and into the big one.
screen: `FROZEN AT THE STEPS.` → `WHERE DO I GO FIRST?` → `A NEW WEEK: TEMPLE AND COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: The Hindi word is mandir, from the Sanskrit mandira: a dwelling, a house. That's the key. A temple is understood as a home where the divine lives, in the form of the murti, the sacred image, which has been ritually installed and is cared for every day: woken, bathed, dressed, fed, and put to rest at night. You're not walking into an auditorium. You're visiting someone's house. That's why everybody first takes off their shoes; there's usually a rack by the door. Many people wash their hands, sometimes their feet. Then, often, they ring the bell hanging at the entrance: your ghanta, announcing that you've arrived. At the heart of the temple is the innermost shrine, the garbhagriha, the womb-house: small, often dark, lit by lamps, with the main image inside. In many temples, only priests go in. Everyone else stands at the threshold, looks, and bows. Above it rises the tower, which you can often see from the street. Many temples have smaller shrines too, for other forms of the divine, and people visit them in turn. There's often no single service everyone arrives for: people come and go when they like, though arti times draw a crowd. A few quiet customs: dress modestly, don't point your feet at the shrine when you sit, and ask before taking photos. Many temples welcome visitors of any background; some admit only Hindus. And if you're unsure, do what a guest does anywhere. Shoes off, watch, and follow.

133.title: Darshan
133.howItsDone: Hindus go to temples for darshan, standing before the murti with folded hands to see the deity and be seen in return; many also speak of taking darshan of saints, sacred rivers and holy places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mandir, the temple as a house where someone lives. Your line was shoes off.

Ask a Hindu friend why they're going to the temple, and they may not say to pray. They may say, I'm going for darshan. People travel for days and stand in lines for hours at famous temples, all for a few seconds at the front. Then the line moves on, and they leave happy. From outside, it can look puzzling. You waited six hours for three seconds? But ask what happened in those three seconds and they'll tell you: I saw. And I was seen. Yesterday you walked up to the threshold. Today, what happens there.
screen: `SIX HOURS IN LINE.` → `THREE SECONDS AT THE FRONT.` → `I SAW, AND I WAS SEEN.`

segments.voice: Darshan comes from the Sanskrit root drish, to see: seeing, a sight, a vision. But in a temple it means something specific: to stand in the presence of the divine and look, and to be looked at in return. That second half is the surprise. Many Hindus understand the murti as truly inhabited, so the seeing goes both ways. That's why the eyes of the image matter so much. On many murtis the eyes are large, bright, sometimes made of silver or painted wide open. In the rites that install a new image, the eyes are often among the last things opened, and after that, the image is said to see. Some temples draw a curtain across the shrine at certain times, and when it opens, the crowd leans forward: darshan! Hands come together. Some people say a name under their breath. Some just look. You can take darshan of more than an image, too: a holy person, a sacred river, a mountain. Wherever the holy is present, you can go to see it and be seen. One more thing a scholar might tell you. The classical schools of Hindu philosophy are called darshanas, ways of seeing. So the same word covers a glance in a temple and a whole system of philosophy. In both, the point is to see clearly. Three seconds can be enough, if you actually look.
screen: `DARSHAN — FROM DRISH, TO SEE.` · `TO SEE, AND TO BE SEEN.` · `THE EYES ARE OPENED LAST.` · `DARSHANAS: WAYS OF SEEING.`

segments.voice: Let your gaze rest softly on an image that matters to you, the murti in your corner, a picture of a deity, a photo of a teacher or someone you love, or simply the sky out the window, especially on the eyes if there are eyes. Don't analyze it; just look, the way you'd look at someone you've missed. Then turn it around and stay with both: what would it be like to be seen like this, fully, without judgment?
Darshan. Seeing: standing before the divine, a holy person or a holy place, to see and to be seen in return. Today's word.
Your line: see. Look, and let yourself be looked at in return. Day one hundred thirty-three.
